Chalcedonian Definition
kal-suh-DOH-nee-uhn def-ih-NISH-uhn
noun (doctrine / church history)
From Chalcedon, the city near Constantinople where the fourth ecumenical council met in 451, + definition (Latin definire, to mark the bounds); the council's settled statement of the person of Christ.

Biblical Definition

The Chalcedonian Definition is the statement of the person of Christ set forth by the Council of Chalcedon in A.D. 451, the fourth ecumenical council, and received ever since by Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant alike as the boundary-stone of orthodox Christology. Against Nestorius, who so divided the two natures as to make two persons, and against Eutyches, who so mingled them as to swallow the human in the divine, the council confessed one and the same Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, of a reasonable soul and body; consubstantial with the Father as to His Godhead and consubstantial with us as to His manhood; to be acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation. The two natures are not blended into a third thing, nor are they torn into two persons; the distinction of natures is preserved, and both concur in one person and one subsistence. These four negatives — without confusion, change, division, separation — are the four walls that guard the mystery of the incarnation. This dictionary confesses the Chalcedonian Definition without reservation as a faithful drawing-out of what the Scriptures teach of the God-man, and the 1689 Confession rests on it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The fourth ecumenical council's statement (A.D. 451) of the person of Christ: one Son, truly God and truly man, in two natures — without confusion, change, division, or separation. The boundary-stone of orthodox Christology, confessed by the whole church.

CHALCEDONIAN DEFINITION, noun. The Christological statement of the Council of Chalcedon, A.D. 451.

Confesses one Son, Jesus Christ, perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man.

He is consubstantial with the Father in Godhead and consubstantial with us in manhood.

Acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation.

Received by the whole church as the boundary of orthodox Christology.

Key Scripture

John 1:14 — "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth."

Phil 2:6 — "Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God."

Col 2:9 — "For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily."

Heb 2:17 — "Wherefore in all things it behoved him to be made like unto his brethren, that he might be a merciful and faithful high priest in things pertaining to God."

Modern Corruption

Every age finds a way to refuse the God-man — ancient heresies divided or mingled His natures; modern liberalism reduces Him to a good man only, and the prosperity and progressive pulpits make Him a symbol, a coach, or a projection of the self — all of them denying the one Lord Chalcedon confessed.

expand to see more

Chalcedon was framed against two corruptions still with us. Nestorianism so separated the natures as to deny that the one who suffered was God in the flesh; modern theologies that speak of a merely human Jesus indwelt by the divine repeat its error. Eutychianism so mingled the natures as to make a third hybrid thing that is neither God nor man; modern theologies that dissolve Christ's true humanity into a vague divinity repeat its error. The four negatives — without confusion, change, division, separation — cut off both.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the council's text, but it faces the constant pressure to reduce the incarnate Lord to something the age can manage: a moral teacher, a liberator-figure, a screen for the self. The principle to recover is the full confession: the Word was made flesh (John 1:14), in Him dwells all the fulness of the Godhead bodily (Col 2:9), yet He was made like His brethren in all things (Heb 2:17). Salvation hangs on this — only one who is truly God and truly man could reconcile God and man.

Hebrew Roots

From Chalcedon (the council city) + Latin definire (to mark the bounds); the 451 confession of one Christ in two unconfused, unmingled natures.
